summary: Describes the problem of encrypting the Server Name Indication (SNI) field in TLS, which currently reveals the site a client is visiting. It lists known attacks, discusses the existing HTTP co-tenancy approach, and sets out requirements for future TLS-layer solutions.

plainLanguage.summary: When you mail a letter, the address is on the outside. This explains why hiding the website name inside secure connections is tricky and what a good fix needs.

questions: why is sni not encrypted in tls
what are the requirements for encrypted sni
what is the cut and paste attack on sni encryption
subtitle: Why hiding the website name in a TLS handshake is harder than it sounds, and what a good fix must do.

tldr.problem: The Server Name Indication (SNI) in a TLS handshake is sent in cleartext, so anyone watching the network can see which site a client is visiting, even when DNS and the data stream are encrypted.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC does not define a solution. It lists the attacks that sank earlier SNI encryption proposals, reviews the existing HTTP co-tenancy (domain fronting) workaround, and sets out requirements that a future TLS-layer solution should meet.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational guide for evaluating designs. The RFC itself warns that no solution may meet every requirement and that practical solutions will have to make compromises.

facts.label: Requirements listed
facts.value: Section 3: cut-and-paste, shared secrets, DoS, sticking out, forward secrecy, multi-party contexts, multiple protocols

today: RFC 8744 is an Informational document and the data lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes the problem and requirements rather than a protocol, so it is a checklist for evaluating SNI encryption designs.

sections.title: The Problem With a Cleartext Name
sections.content:
Watchers of web traffic used to have three main windows: DNS requests, IP addresses in packet headers, and the data stream itself. Those windows are closing. More traffic is encrypted with TLS, DNS over TLS and DNS over HTTPS hide lookups, and cloud and CDN platforms put many services behind a few IP addresses.

Multiplexed servers still need to know which service a client wants, so they rely on the Server Name Indication (SNI) TLS extension. It travels in cleartext in the ClientHello message. As the other channels close, monitoring focuses on the SNI.

The RFC does not present a solution. It gives guidelines for judging proposals, and says the review of HTTP-level solutions is not an endorsement of them.
sections.plainLanguage: The website name is like the address on an envelope. Everything inside is sealed, but the address is still visible to the mail carrier.

sections.title: History and Uses of the SNI
sections.content:
The SNI extension was specified in 2003 in RFC 3546 to help manage colocation servers, where several services share one IP address. Only the hostname variant, which carries a domain name, was ever specified and deployed. The current specification is RFC 6066.

Middlebox developers found uses the designers had not anticipated, including censoring services, parental controls and phishing blocks, assigning different QoS to target services, enterprise firewalls blocking sites, and exempting healthcare or financial sites from man-in-the-middle inspection. The RFC also notes the SNI is probably part of the metadata collected by pervasive surveillance actors.

Encrypting the SNI would thwart most of these uses, but it also breaks or weakens those middlebox practices. The RFC says most of the functions can be done another way, such as opt-in DNS filtering, packet marking for per-stream QoS, or software on enterprise computers.
sections.plainLanguage: People who run networks found out they could read the address on the envelope and use it for all sorts of things, some helpful and some not. Hiding it takes away both kinds.

sections.title: Attacks a Design Must Withstand
sections.content:
Many proposals looked promising but were rejected after security review found attacks. The RFC collects them as requirements.

  • Mitigate cut-and-paste attacks. If the SNI is simply replaced by an encrypted value, an adversary can copy it into its own connection to the multiplexed server, which then contacts the protected service and reveals its identity through its certificate.
  • Avoid widely shared secrets. A symmetric key known to every user is fragile, because one compromised user compromises the whole set.
  • Prevent SNI-based denial of service. Random encrypted values could force a resource-limited front-end to waste effort on decryption attempts.
  • Do not stick out. If SNI encryption is easy to detect, it can be blocked or its users flagged.
  • Maintain forward secrecy. If the SNI key derives from the server's public key, a later key compromise exposes the SNI in archived connections.
sections.plainLanguage: A sneaky person could copy your sealed envelope and see where it gets delivered. A good design must stop that, must not use one password for everybody, and must not make secret letters look different from ordinary ones.

sections.title: Trust, Protocols and Transports
sections.content:
If a fronting service relays traffic to the protected service, the design must decide who verifies whom. With one handshake verified only against the fronting service's certificate, the client is exposed to a MITM attack by that service. If the protected service's certificate is verified, the client no longer verifies the fronting service, which allows a spoofed fronting service to act as a honeypot. The RFC concludes that end-to-end TLS to the protected service is preferable, but the fronting service should also be authenticated.

The requirement is wider than HTTP. SMTP, DNS, IMAP and XMPP also use TLS, so an application-agnostic solution in the TLS layer is needed. The RFC also says it is desirable to hide the ALPN values, though this may be better done independently of the SNI, and the mechanism should work with DTLS and QUIC, not only TLS over TCP.
sections.plainLanguage: If a helper passes your letter along, you need to be sure the helper is honest and is not a fake. And the secret-address trick has to work for every kind of mail, not only one kind.

sections.title: HTTP Co-tenancy Fronting
sections.content:
Without a TLS-level fix, many sites use HTTP co-tenancy, often called domain fronting. The TLS connection goes to the fronting server (for example, SNI fronting.example.com) and HTTP requests over it are directed at the hidden service (hidden.example.com). It needs no change to TLS, but the client must discover the hidden service, the browser must be directed to use it, the client has no cryptographic proof that content comes from the hidden service, and it protects only HTTP.

Tunneling HTTPS inside HTTPS, with the fronting server acting like an HTTP proxy, gives an end-to-end connection to the hidden server, but needs double encryption and makes the fronting server relay messages. The RFC also covers delegation control, meaning how to say which fronting servers are acceptable, and mentions the HTTP/2 ORIGIN frame (RFC 8336) and secondary certificate authentication as related work.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of hiding the address, you send the letter to a big building everyone knows, and inside someone passes it to the right office. It works, but you have to trust the building.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC lists attacks against SNI encryption and requirements to mitigate them, and says current HTTP-based solutions meet only some of them. It states that no solution may meet every requirement and practical solutions will have to make compromises.

In particular, the requirement not to stick out may have to be lifted, especially for solutions that could quickly reach large-scale deployment. Encrypting the SNI will also reduce the efficacy of middlebox practices, so alternative solutions will have to be developed. The document has no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: No perfect fix exists, so people may have to accept a few trade-offs. Hiding the address will also stop some helpful mail checks, so those will need new ways to work.
